title: Improving Lipid Nanoparticles for mRNA Delivery
research_problem: How can lipid nanoparticle formulations be optimised to improve the delivery of mRNA into target cells?
proposed_research: Develop a series of lipid nanoparticle formulations with different compositions and compare their particle size, dispersity, encapsulation efficiency and transfection performance in cell-based models.
why_it_matters: mRNA therapies depend on effective delivery into cells. Improving delivery efficiency could reduce the amount of therapeutic material required and support the development of more effective nucleic-acid-based treatments.
existing_evidence: The lab has previously investigated lipid nanoparticle composition and its relationship with transfection performance and has experience producing and characterising lipid-based delivery systems.
relevant_lab_capabilities: Lipid nanoparticle formulation, nucleic-acid encapsulation, particle-size and dispersity analysis, cell culture and transfection experiments.

title: Understanding Nanoparticle Structure and Long-Term Stability
research_problem: How do changes in the internal structure of nanoparticle formulations during storage affect their stability and subsequent performance?
proposed_research: Study selected nanoparticle formulations under different storage conditions and monitor changes in their physical characteristics and internal structure over time using physicochemical characterisation, electron microscopy and neutron scattering.
why_it_matters: A promising formulation has limited practical value if its properties change significantly during storage. Understanding the mechanisms behind these changes could support the development of more stable drug-delivery systems.
existing_evidence: Previous work by the lab has identified structural changes in nanoparticle formulations under different formulation and storage conditions.
relevant_lab_capabilities: Nanoparticle formulation, stability assessment, particle-size and dispersity analysis, scanning and transmission electron microscopy, with neutron-scattering access through external collaborations.

title: Predicting Cellular Uptake from Nanoparticle Characteristics
research_problem: Can measurable physical characteristics of nanoparticles help predict how effectively they will be taken up by cells?
proposed_research: Produce a diverse set of nanoparticle formulations, characterise their physical properties, measure cellular uptake using imaging, and analyse relationships between formulation characteristics and biological performance.
why_it_matters: Identifying characteristics associated with successful cellular uptake could help researchers prioritise promising formulations earlier and reduce unnecessary biological testing.
existing_evidence: The lab's previous imaging work has shown differences in cellular uptake between experimental nanoparticle formulations and has generated experience linking physicochemical measurements with biological behaviour.
relevant_lab_capabilities: Nanoparticle formulation, physicochemical characterisation, mammalian cell culture, cellular uptake studies, imaging and quantitative image analysis.

title: Targeted Nanoparticle Delivery to Diseased Cells
research_problem: Can nanoparticle surfaces be modified to improve preferential delivery of therapeutic payloads to specific diseased cell populations?
proposed_research: Develop surface-modified nanoparticle formulations and compare their uptake against non-targeted formulations in appropriate cell models, examining whether the modifications improve preferential cellular delivery.
why_it_matters: More selective delivery could increase therapeutic activity at the intended site while reducing unnecessary exposure elsewhere.
existing_evidence: The lab has extensive experience developing nanoparticle formulations and measuring cellular uptake, but targeted delivery would represent an expansion of its existing research.
relevant_lab_capabilities: Nanoparticle formulation, physicochemical characterisation, cell culture, cellular uptake studies and imaging. Additional targeting expertise or collaboration may be required

title: Effect of lipid nanoparticle surface modifications on delivery into diseased cells
research_problem: Unclear whether changing the surface properties of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) can increase entry into diseased cells and increase the amount of RNA payload actually delivered intracellularly. Key unknowns include which surface modifications improve cell interactions and delivery efficiency, and which disease-relevant cell model(s) to test.
proposed_research: Perform a comparative study testing LNPs with different surface modifications to assess how those changes affect (a) interaction with target cells, (b) cellular uptake, and (c) functional intracellular delivery of an RNA payload. Specific surface chemistries or ligands to compare: Not yet provided. Specific disease model or cell type to represent "diseased cells": Not yet provided. Outcome measures (e.g., uptake quantification, transfection efficiency, RNA bioactivity): Not yet provided.
why_it_matters: If surface modifications can be identified that increase uptake and functional RNA delivery into disease-relevant cells, formulations could be prioritised for further therapeutic development. Understanding these relationships could improve targeting, increase efficacy and reduce required doses for nucleic-acid therapies.
existing_evidence: From the rough note: the proposer currently works with lipid nanoparticles and cellular uptake but has not specified prior data for the specific surface modifications or disease model. From the lab profile: the Advanced Drug Delivery Laboratory has prior projects on optimising LNP composition for nucleic-acid delivery, investigating relationships between formulation characteristics and transfection performance, and imaging differences in cellular uptake between formulations. No preliminary experimental data specific to the proposed surface-modification comparisons or to a chosen disease model has been provided.
relevant_lab_capabilities: In-house: preparation of lipid-based nanoparticle formulations; encapsulation of therapeutic payloads (nucleic acids); formulation optimisation; particle-size and dispersity measurement; encapsulation and stability assessment; mammalian cell culture; transfection experiments; cellular uptake studies; quantitative imaging analysis; scanning and transmission electron microscopy. External access (via collaborations): neutron-scattering and other specialist structural-characterisation facilities.

title: pH‑responsive nanoparticle formulation for tumour‑microenvironment‑triggered drug release
research_problem: Design a nanoparticle formulation that remains relatively stable under normal (physiological) conditions but increases release of its therapeutic payload when exposed to tumour‑associated conditions (example stimulus: lower pH). The proposer is unsure whether the lab has appropriate tumour models or specific expertise in stimulus‑responsive materials for this work.
proposed_research: Develop and characterise nanoparticle formulations that show low drug release at physiological pH and increased release at acidic pH representative of tumour microenvironments. Key planned activities: (a) formulation development and optimisation (e.g. lipid‑based or other nanoparticle systems), (b) physicochemical characterisation (particle size, dispersity, encapsulation efficiency, stability), (c) in vitro release testing under different pH conditions to quantify stimulus‑responsive release, (d) cell‑based evaluation of cellular uptake and biological activity in cultured mammalian cells, and (e) imaging/structural analysis (SEM/TEM, quantitative imaging). Important details not yet provided: identity of the therapeutic payload, the precise stimulus mechanism/material chemistry to confer pH responsiveness, and which tumour models (in vitro or in vivo) would be used.
why_it_matters: A nanoparticle that selectively increases drug release in tumour microenvironments could improve on‑target delivery to tumour tissue and reduce systemic exposure/toxicity. Demonstrating controllable stimulus‑responsive release would inform formulation design rules that link nanoparticle properties with biologically relevant release profiles and delivery performance.
existing_evidence: From the lab profile: the group has experience in nanoparticle formulation and optimisation (including lipid‑based systems and encapsulation), comprehensive physicochemical characterisation (particle size, dispersity, encapsulation, stability), imaging and structural analysis (SEM, TEM, quantitative imaging; access to neutron‑scattering facilities via collaborators), and biological evaluation in mammalian cell culture (transfection experiments, cellular uptake studies). Example previous projects documented in the profile include optimisation of lipid nanoparticles for nucleic‑acid delivery, studies linking nanoparticle structure with stability using imaging and neutron scattering, and imaging of cellular uptake across formulations. Not yet provided: direct prior work on stimulus‑responsive (e.g. pH‑sensitive) materials or demonstrated testing in tumour models.
relevant_lab_capabilities: In‑house/formulation: preparation of nanoparticle drug‑delivery systems, lipid‑based nanoparticle formulation, encapsulation of therapeutic payloads, formulation optimisation. Physicochemical characterisation: particle‑size measurement, dispersity analysis, encapsulation assessment, stability assessment. Imaging/structural analysis: scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), quantitative imaging analysis; access to neutron‑scattering facilities through external collaborations. Biological evaluation: mammalian cell culture, transfection experiments, cellular uptake studies, comparison of formulation performance in cell‑based models. Collaboration/environment: interdisciplinary collaborations across pharmaceutical sciences, materials science, biomedical imaging and molecular/cellular biology; external facility access for specialist structural characterisation. Capability gaps/uncertainties: specific expertise in stimulus‑responsive materials is not confirmed (Not yet provided), and suitable tumour models for testing stimulus‑responsive release are not specified (Not yet provided).

title: Effect of particle size, lipid composition and surface properties on nanoparticle transport across blood–brain barrier models
research_problem: The blood–brain barrier (BBB) limits delivery of therapeutics to the brain. The investigator proposes to determine how nanoparticle design variables — particle size, lipid composition and surface properties — influence transport across a BBB model to inform design of nanoparticles that cross the BBB more effectively for neurological disease treatment.
proposed_research: Design and prepare a panel of lipid-based nanoparticle formulations that systematically vary particle size, lipid composition and surface surface chemistry. Perform physicochemical characterisation (particle size, dispersity, encapsulation, stability) and structural imaging (SEM/TEM) for each formulation. Evaluate transport and cellular uptake using an in vitro blood–brain barrier model (specific BBB model type and source: Not yet provided). Quantify translocation across the barrier and uptake by brain-relevant cells, and correlate transport metrics with measured nanoparticle properties to identify design features that enhance BBB transport. Key missing details that need to be specified before work starts: choice of BBB model (e.g., transwell co-culture, iPSC-derived barrier, primary cells), therapeutic payload (if any), whether in vitro findings will be followed by in vivo studies, and which brain cell types or disease contexts to target (all: Not yet provided).
why_it_matters: Improving nanoparticle transport across the BBB could enable more effective delivery of therapeutics for neurological diseases. Systematically linking nanoparticle physicochemical properties to BBB transport would provide design rules for nanoparticles intended to reach the brain, helping prioritise formulations for further preclinical development.
existing_evidence: From the researcher’s note: interest in varying size, lipid composition and surface properties to study BBB transport; uncertainty about available BBB models and neurological-disease expertise. From the lab profile: the Advanced Drug Delivery Laboratory has prior, relevant experience in lipid-based nanoparticle formulation, optimisation, physicochemical characterisation and studies of cellular uptake. Example prior projects in the lab profile include optimisation of lipid nanoparticles for nucleic-acid delivery, studies linking nanoparticle structure with stability, and imaging of cellular uptake. No direct evidence in the note or lab profile that the lab has previously used blood–brain barrier models or conducted neurological-disease-specific studies — Not yet provided.
relevant_lab_capabilities: Preparation of nanoparticle drug-delivery systems; lipid-based nanoparticle formulation; encapsulation of payloads; formulation optimisation; particle-size measurement and dispersity analysis; encapsulation and stability assessment; scanning electron microscopy and transmission electron microscopy; quantitative imaging analysis; mammalian cell culture; transfection experiments; cellular uptake studies; access to specialist structural-characterisation facilities (external collaborations) including neutron-scattering through collaborators. Not yet provided: confirmed availability of an in vitro or in vivo blood–brain barrier model and in-house neurological disease expertise.
